hero.eyebrow: A short economics lesson on price changes
hero.titleLine1: How much more expensive is the basket?
hero.intro: Compare two national quarterly indices over the same period: one tracks prices paid by households, the other tracks wage prices for a comparable mix of jobs. Rebase each series to 100 at the starting quarter, then see where they go.
hero.noteBody: Index levels depend on their reference period. Here we compare percentage changes, not the raw index points.

learning.title: The two lines answer different questions
learning.cpiTitle: How much more do household purchases cost overall?
learning.cpiBody: The CPI summarises price changes for goods and services households commonly buy, weighted by their importance in household spending. The Australian national series is a weighted average of the eight capital cities. Every household has a different basket, so the CPI is not your personal bill.
learning.wpiTitle: How have wage prices changed for similar jobs?
learning.wpiBody: The WPI tracks wage price changes for a comparable mix of jobs, aiming to exclude changes in job content, quantity and quality. This chart uses the original index for total hourly rates of pay excluding bonuses. It does not describe any person's pay, hours, bonuses or after-tax income.
learning.normalizeTitle: Different reference periods: compare percentage changes
learning.normalizeBody: An index reference period is just the starting point for its scale. We set both selected starting quarters to 100; later values show each series' change from that point. The gap between the lines is the difference in cumulative index growth, not a difference in any person's purchasing power.
learning.normalizeLink: The comparable measures are trends and changes over the selected period.
